extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of English/literary criticism; critics, poets, and general readers learning to read and judge poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for close-reading, interpreting, and judging poems, drawn from I. A. Richards' Practical Criticism. Covers what to notice (sense, sound, form, imagery, intention), common errors, and recommended reading methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making out the plain sense of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The difficulty of making out the poem's plain, overt prose sense — its intelligible meaning as a set of ordinary English sentences — and also apprehending its feeling, tone and intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many readers (even good or devoted ones) frequently fail to construe poems' prose sense; failure to construe can lead to travesty in paraphrase. Treat 'construing' like a school exercise: paraphrase and test that the plain sense is clear before moving to poetic significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensuous apprehension (form and rhythm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words in sequence have form to the mind's ear and tongue; the mind perceives movement and rhythm which are essential to poetic reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers differ greatly in natural perception of rhythm; some must build rhythm laboriously. Attend to rhythm as a perceptible movement — read aloud or slowly when necessary. Distinguish inherent rhythm (the poem's necessary skeletal movement) from an ascribed rhythm imposed by reader prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagery and visualisation
rubrics_metrics.description: The role and place of imagery (especially visual imagery) in reading poetry, and differences in readers' capacities to visualise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that some readers rely heavily on images while others do not; images are erratic and personal. Be wary of judging a poem solely by images it evokes in you; test whether imagery is relevant to sense and feeling of the poem rather than merely mnemonic or associative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four aspects of meaning: sense, feeling, tone, intention
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaning in poetry operates in four aspects: sense (prose content), feeling (affective content), tone (attitudinal colouring), and intention (authorial or purposive stance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse these aspects separately and note their relative subordinations (e.g., scientific writing vs political speeches vs poetry). Confusion between them causes many critical errors; map out which aspect is dominant in any passage before judging value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figurative language: metaphor, personification and literalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Causes of misunderstanding arising from figurative language; the tension between literalism and metaphor; mixture in metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish intuitive readings from over-literal ones. Recognise poetic licence but beware mixed or muddled metaphor. Analyse whether personification or metaphor aids communication of sense/feeling or merely decorates. Use careful paraphrase to test figurative readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic form and prosody (inherent vs ascribed rhythm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty apprehending poetic form due to bad assumptions (the 'regularity myth') and the need to recognise variation about a norm; rhythm often goes deeper than mere audible regularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming mechanical regularity; seek the inherent rhythmic 'skeleton' of a poem. Attend to prosody, metre, and underlying rhythmic organization; do not neglect sound as merely ornamental. Read aloud and practise slow reading to apprehend form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence of form and content (unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The critical requirement that form correspond to content — that poetic shape should fit the meaning and feeling communicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a passage, ask whether chosen form (verse, stanza, rhythm, diction) supports, contradicts, or undermines the sense and feeling. Unity and appropriate correspondence are signs of technical fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stock responses and irrelevant associations
rubrics_metrics.description: The omnipresence of habitual or 'stock' responses and irrelevant associations (mnemonic irrelevancies) that distort reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify stock responses (conventional emotional reflexes, clichés, familiar subject-responses) and demarcate their proper field. Recognise their utility but be alert to their distortion of judgement. Compare responses across readers and contexts to see whether they are intrinsic to the poem or extraneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimentality and inhibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentimentality as an abusive gesture (vague thought, over-facile emotion, or crude response) and inhibition as its complement; causes, varieties and cures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose whether a response or passage is sentimental (over-persistence of sentiment, conventional metaphors) or inhibited (excessive restraint); evaluate subject and treatment. Consider whether the emotional response is justified by the poem's sense. The book offers discussion of causes and therapeutic teaching methods to reduce sentimentality and undue inhibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine in poetry and the problem of belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Tension between readers' and poets' beliefs (doctrinal content) and the difficulty of reconciling intellectual and emotional assumptions in interpreting poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate intellectual vs emotional assumptions and the 'justification' appropriate to each. Beware of ascribing insincerity too quickly; evaluate sincerity as absence of self-deception and as genuineness. Consider spontaneity versus sophistication and how doctrine affects reception rather than immediate poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical presuppositions and critical preconceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical expectations, preconceptions and dogmas (e.g., subject/message tests, the 'lilt' quest) that bias reading; confusion between means and ends; the 'summation of details' blunder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose and question technical presuppositions before applying them. Recognise that critical theories are often ambiguous and can disable judgment if applied as infallible rules. Use principles only as protective aids and not as substitutes for perception and discernment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between statement and expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminological distinction: 'statement' for utterances whose primary interest is what they say (propositional meaning), and 'expression' for utterances where the mental operations of the writer are to be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the distinction in mind when analysing protocols and critical statements: sometimes we must investigate what an opinion states; other times we must study how the opinion came about (expression). This distinction aids more fruitful investigation than mere argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of reading: multiple and slow readings, reading aloud, paraphrase
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended practical techniques for arriving at sound judgments: multiple readings, recording number of readings, slow reading, reading aloud, paraphrase and definition techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Richards' experiment had readers make multiple readings (often 4+ and up to 10–12) and to note them; thoroughness produces more reliable judgments. Use dictionary and definition techniques to pin down sense; read aloud to apprehend rhythm and sound; paraphrase to test plain sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to sound: music, rhyme, cacophony, onomatopoeia
rubrics_metrics.description: Sound-related criteria — how musical qualities, rhyme, cacophony, onomatopoeia and the correspondence of sound and sense affect poetic meaning and emotional effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse correspondences of sound and sense; beware of careless assumptions that musicality equals poetic value. Evaluate whether sonic effects serve the poem's sense and feeling rather than being mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of psychology and protocols for documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of collecting anonymous 'protocols' (readers' written comments) as fieldwork in comparative ideology; psychology as an indispensable instrument for elucidating how readers form opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and compare many independent written responses to the same poems to reveal common confusions and stock responses. Use psychology cautiously (avoid abuse/profanation) to dissect and order motives, but expect only a superficial beginning from such protocols — they supply accessible starting materials for further research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical principles as aids, not substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Maxims and rules of criticism can help avoid blunders but must never substitute for discernment; applied crudely they mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat watchwords ('Poetry is expression', 'Poetry is imitation') as ambiguous pointers; always test principles against the poem itself. Remember that great principles help wise readers but become will-o'-the-wisps for fools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding preconceptions, authority, and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical errors arising from preconceptions, undue appeal to authority, and variability in taste and response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate humility and awareness of subjectivity. Recognise variability among readers and avoid appealing to authority to resolve textual ambiguities; instead, map out differing legitimate readings and test them against textual evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and pedagogy: teaching English to improve construal and discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational recommendations to remedy defects in reading: teach construal (ability to make out plain sense), improve speech and prose competence, and develop habits that reduce critical fog.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise practical exercises (protocols, repeated readings, paraphrase, close attention to diction and prosody) in English teaching. Encourage slow, disciplined reading and exercises to reduce stock responses and sentimentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of irrelevant mnemonic pulls and conservations
rubrics_metrics.description: The need to distinguish mnemonic pulls (associations with other poems, political/temporal concerns, familiar stock subjects) from what the poem actually says.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a reader's response invokes extraneous topical or mnemonic material (e.g., royalism, socialism, etc.), test whether such associations are relevant to the poem's internal meaning; bracket them when they obstruct construal.
